issues.legal_issue: A court may set aside a confirmed court-supervised liquidation sale and direct a fresh sale when the confirmed price is grossly inadequate and a bona fide higher offer is made before the property is transferred.
material_facts: The assets of the company in liquidation were advertised for sale, and Divya’s offer was increased from Rs. 37 lakhs to Rs. 1.30 crores before the sale was confirmed in its favour.
Within days of confirmation, Sharma and Jay offered Rs. 2 crores each and deposited Rs. 40 lakhs each to demonstrate their bona fides.
The offers of Rs. 2 crores showed that the confirmed price was grossly inadequate; neither possession nor a sale deed had been transferred to Divya.
The sale conditions empowered the court to set aside a confirmed sale in the interests of creditors and others or in the public interest.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in setting aside the confirmed sale and directing a fresh sale; the appeals challenging that decision were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Rule 273 of the Companies (Court) Rules, 1959, acceptance of an offer subject to court confirmation gives the offeror no vested right to automatic confirmation. The court must satisfy itself that the price is adequate, even without fraud or irregularity, because it safeguards the interests of the company and its creditors. A higher bona fide offer and a grossly inadequate confirmed price can justify setting aside the sale. The Court relied on Navalkha and Sons v. Sri Ramanya Das, LICA (P) Ltd. v. Official Liquidator (1) and (2), and the principles discussed in Navalkha from Gordhan Das Chuni Lal v. T. Sriman Kanthimathinatha Pillai, Rathnaswami Pillai v. Sadapathy Pillai, S. Soundarajan v. M/s Roshan & Co., and A. Subbaraya Mudaliar v. K. Sundararajan. The sale conditions also expressly permitted setting aside a confirmed sale in the stated interests.

rule.if: court_supervised_liquidation_sale and challenge_to_confirmed_sale and confirmed_sale and grossly_inadequate_price and bona_fide_higher_offer and transfer_not_completed and sale_terms_allow_cancellation

predicates.court_supervised_liquidation_sale: A court supervised the sale of assets belonging to a company in liquidation.
predicates.challenge_to_confirmed_sale: A party challenged the court’s decision concerning a sale after the sale had been confirmed.
predicates.confirmed_sale: The court confirmed the sale in favour of a purchaser.
predicates.grossly_inadequate_price: The confirmed price was substantially below the value indicated by a higher available offer.
predicates.bona_fide_higher_offer: A prospective purchaser made a substantially higher offer and took steps demonstrating the seriousness of that offer.
predicates.transfer_not_completed: Possession of the assets had not been handed over and the sale deed had not been executed.
predicates.sale_terms_allow_cancellation: The conditions governing the sale stated that the court could set it aside after confirmation in specified interests.

issues.definition: When a court-supervised liquidation sale has been confirmed but the price is grossly inadequate, a bona fide higher offer is made, the transfer is incomplete, and the sale terms permit cancellation, the court may set aside the sale and order a fresh one.

issues.legal_issue: A court does not become functus officio upon confirming a court-supervised liquidation sale when the sale conditions preserve its authority to set aside the sale and the transfer has not been completed.
material_facts: The sale conditions expressly reserved the court’s power to set aside the sale even after confirmation.
The court confirmed the sale in favour of Divya, but neither possession nor a sale deed had been transferred to it when the applications to reopen the sale were made.
issues.conclusion: The High Court had authority to consider setting aside the confirmed sale and was not functus officio.
issues.legal_principle: The express sale condition allowing the court to set aside a confirmed sale preserved its authority to act in the specified interests. Since possession had not been handed over and the sale deed had not been executed, confirmation did not prevent the court from intervening. The Court relied on the sale condition and the principles in Navalkha and Sons v. Sri Ramanya Das and LICA (P) Ltd. v. Official Liquidator (1) and (2).

predicates.confirmed_sale: The court confirmed the sale in favour of a purchaser.
predicates.sale_terms_allow_cancellation: The conditions governing the sale stated that the court could set it aside after confirmation in specified interests.

issues.definition: When a court confirms a court-supervised liquidation sale under terms allowing cancellation and the transfer remains incomplete, the court retains authority to reconsider the sale.
